title: Hanson’s call to go early into super cash
full_text:
Cash-strapped Australians should be allowed easier access to their superannuation before they retire, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has proposed, pitting her party against Labor over the regulation of the country’s $4.4 trillion retirement savings system.
Though the policy remains in development, the proposal sparked immediate condemnation from Jim Chalmers and the superannuation sector after it was floated on Sunday by Senator Hanson, who said savings could be tapped to cover mortgage repayments and living expenses.
“A lot of Australians are doing it tough now and struggling to pay off their mortgages,” she said in an interview with News24. “In some ways, I feel you should give them their money now, and let them help them with the cost of living. It is their money; they’ve sacrificed it in lieu of pay. So, in a lot of cases, people want it.” Early access to superannuation before retirement is already permitted under extremely narrow circumstances, such as covering the cost of medical treatment, funeral expenses and preventing the foreclosure or forced sale of an individual’s primary home; it requires sign-off from the Australian Taxation Office.
Access because of to financial hardship, permanent or temporary incapacity or a terminal medical condition is also allowed.
Branding Australia’s superannuation system as “broken”, Senator Hanson called for early access rules to be “lightened up a bit” so people could tap their savings “in times of crisis”.
One Nation’s Treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce confirmed that work on the minor party’s early superannuation access policy was ongoing, with details over eligibility and limits on withdrawals to be determined.
Despite the lack of detail surrounding the measure, the federal Treasurer lashed the proposal, claiming One Nation would “decimate” Australia’s retirement savings system and leave Australians worse off without compounding investment returns.
“This is the single biggest threat to the superannuation system in four decades,” he said in a statement. “They will end super as we know it and workers will be poorer as a consequence.” During the pandemic, the Morrison government established an early release superannuation scheme that allowed people who had lost their jobs or had hours cut to withdraw up to $20,000 from their accounts in two $10,000 tranches. Analysis by the superannuation industry subsequently found those who accessed the scheme would face a cumulative $83.8bn shortfall in their retirement savings due to lower investment earnings.
Senator Hanson’s comments similarly attracted criticism from the superannuation sector, with Mary Delahunty, chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, saying the policy would be “extremely damaging” and increase reliance on the Age Pension.
Citing the Coalition’s ill-fated push to enable first-home buyers and some separated women to tap superannuation for a house deposit – which had similarly been supported by One Nation – Ms Delahunty said broadening early access would prove “incredibly unpopular” with voters. “Australians want their retirement money to be providing dignity in their retirement. It is always their money. They pay less tax if they wait. They pay more … if they get it right now. Australians know the deal here.” Former Industry Super Australia chief economist Stephen Anthony, now at Macroeconomics Advisory, said a weakening of existing early access regulations would inevitably raise liquidity risks for superannuation funds. “This is a real problem,” Dr Anthony warned. “Obviously, at the moment they have a very transparent runway to manage liquidity flows … but when you change those arrangements, they need some sort of liquidity stopgap in place so they can manage unforeseen circumstances.”
